reason: The wording survives; the translation date does not. Poetry Chaikhana, read this run, prints the opening as its own two line stanza, Now we will count to twelve / and we will all keep still., with no comma and lower case and at the second line head, and credits Alastair Reid, Extravagaria: A Bilingual Edition, Farrar, Straus and Giroux. So the English is Reid's and the locator the opening two lines is right. But Chaikhana gives NO year, and the verifier's evidence claims both reprints credit a 1974 volume. Only The Marginalian, a blog and not a bibliographic authority, says 1974, and it is wrong: Reid's Extravagaria was first published by Jonathan Cape, London, in 1972, with the first American edition from Farrar, Straus and Giroux in 1974. The National Library of Scotland catalogues Reid's manuscript and typescript of Extravagaria as 1972, or before. The rule asks for the year of the published translation whose wording it uses, and the card as written reads to a morning reader as Reid translated this in 1974, which is false by two years. The verifier dropped an unopened page range as unverified and then kept an unopened year on the same evidence, which is the same fault left standing. Everything else clears: shipped.js returns no match, no near match, Neruda at 0 of 3, not banned; Estravagario 1958 and the translation 1972 are both well inside the pre-2000 line; the poem is in scope, publishable, and squarely on stillness and silence; the source line leads with the name, carries no dash, and runs 93 characters with the fix; Poetry is the form of the work. The fix is one digit. Note should say plainly that the Spanish is A callarse in Estravagario, Losada, 1958, that Reid's translation is of 1972, that the wording was read in online reprints crediting the Farrar, Straus and Giroux bilingual text, and that no printed copy of either volume was opened.
